A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same strategic-robustness work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison; extracted text and rendered pages resolve the relevant content.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and GTSRB experiments comparing clean, strategic, and adversarial training, including opponent-strength and misspecification analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original CIFAR-100, preference-order, utility-inference, and continuous-utility results in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The core minimax framework remains, but v2 adds a non-target penalty for preference attacks (Eq. 12), utility-inference procedures (C.6), and sequential strategic training with alternative fallback attacks (C.7). These extend the actual procedures. The epsilon=0.1 stabilization described in Section 5.1 was already disclosed in v1 Appendix B.4.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10 and GTSRB. Appendix C also evaluates new scenarios involving preference-order and continuous-valued utilities, opponents targeting known gaps in defenses, and recovery of targets and utility matrices from previous attacks.

E2.justification: Clean and PGD-adversarial training remain the principal baselines. New comparisons evaluate prediction-based versus attack-vector-based utility inference (Table 7), and utility-weighted, sequential, sequential-with-adversarial-fallback, multi-targeted, and adversarial training (Table 8), substantially extending the comparison methods.

E3.justification: The original splits, training budgets, and PGD settings are retained. New protocols include average and worst-case targeted evaluations against informed opponents (C.3), epsilon=0.5 for preference training (C.4), target-prediction and matrix-recovery metrics with known k (C.6), and aligned versus misaligned utility orderings (C.7).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's 1-hot strength, semantics, and misspecification analyses, v2 adds sensitivity to larger k (Figures 6 and 9), tests attacks on explicitly undefended targets (C.3), and examines utility-order alignment and fallback choices (C.7). These substantially expand tests of robustness and modeling assumptions.

E5.justification: v1 already reports quantiles and mean/standard-deviation curves. v2 adds standard errors for the random 1-hot comparisons in Table 3 and specifies ten randomly drawn preference orderings with mean/standard-deviation reporting in Table 5. This does not establish additional runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their values, while Figures 6 and 9 and Tables 3–8 add substantial results. For example, Table 6 reports CIFAR-100 anti-semantic VGG accuracy of 20.2 for strategic versus 20.5 for adversarial training. Some new prose disagrees with its table: C.4 claims a 4.1-point VGG gain, whereas Table 5 implies 3.9.

T1.justification: The central formulations and clean–strategic–adversarial inequality remain. v2 adds a formal preference-order utility definition and mathematical reasoning relating continuous utilities to their binary support and target ordering (C.4 and C.7). These are limited formal extensions, without new theorem-and-proof development.

C1.justification: The central claim that incentive knowledge can improve the robustness–accuracy tradeoff remains. v2 additionally advertises preference-order opponents, mentions utility inference, and explicitly claims that misspecification risks are often manageable. Its novelty statement is qualified to multiclass strategic behavior over complex inputs.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of indirect protection across attack targets (C.3), reduced gains when the incentive set approaches the adversarial setting (C.5), and difficulty recovering rarely attacked targets (C.6). It also interprets utility-order alignment effects (C.7) and discloses difficulties obtaining comparable ViT performance (C.1).

D1.justification: Existing optimization, hardware, runtime, and code/checkpoint access statements remain. New details include the preference-training epsilon, CIFAR-100 semantic grouping, and utility inference's observation requirements, known-k assumption, and frequency-based reconstruction rule. These support the extensions without substantially revising the original reproducibility documentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mo et al. (2022) concerning adversarial training of vision transformers and removes Rosenfeld and Rosenfeld (2024), including the connection to strategic classification under unknown costs. It also sharpens positioning relative to predominantly binary, linear, tabular strategic-classification work.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the exposition remain. v2 revises the abstract, introduction examples, risk-tradeoff interpretation, and several results passages, while adding acknowledgments and appendix cross-references. These refine the existing narrative alongside the newly added scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds six result tables and new k-dependent plots, expands opponent illustrations with preferences, and redraws or relabels existing plots. The conceptual panel from v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 2, rather than a new analysis. Document typography, citation presentation, and page layout also change.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's central incentive assumptions through informed-opponent tests, preference and continuous-utility experiments, and utility recovery. The CIFAR-100 exception also establishes a useful boundary on gains. These address important evidentiary gaps in v1, although validation remains controlled and minor prose/table discrepancies, such as C.4 versus Table 5, reduce precision.
